lesson.title: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: The Handshake That Opens Every TCP Connection
lesson.summary: The three way handshake is the exchange of SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK segments that lets both sides of a TCP connection agree on each other's starting sequence number before any application data flows.
lesson.body:
TCP is connection oriented, which means it needs to establish shared state before either side sends application data, and the three way handshake is the specific mechanism that does it, three segments exchanged using the SYN and ACK flags introduced in the TCP segment header.

The reason it takes exactly three messages, not two and not four, comes down to what each side needs to accomplish. Each side has to tell the other its own starting sequence number, called its initial sequence number, or ISN, and each side has to confirm it received the other side's ISN. The ISN itself is chosen pseudo randomly rather than starting from a fixed value like zero, specifically so that an outside attacker cannot easily guess it and inject or hijack data into the connection. Two messages would only synchronize one direction of the conversation. Four messages would be one too many, because the response that confirms the first side's ISN can be combined with the second side's own SYN into a single segment, collapsing what would otherwise be two separate messages into one, which is exactly why the second message of the exchange is called SYN-ACK.

Here is a full worked example with concrete numbers. A client at 203.0.113.10 wants to open a connection to a server at 198.51.100.20 on port 443. First, the client picks an initial sequence number, say ISN_c = 1000, and sends a segment with the SYN flag set, sequence number 1000, and no data. Second, the server picks its own initial sequence number, say ISN_s = 5000, and replies with a segment that has both the SYN and ACK flags set, sequence number 5000, and acknowledgment number 1001, which is the client's ISN plus one, telling the client "I received your starting point of 1000, and I am now expecting byte 1001 from you next." Third, the client replies with a segment that has the ACK flag set, but not SYN this time since a SYN is only needed once per side, with sequence number 1001 and acknowledgment number 5001, confirming it received the server's starting point of 5000 and is expecting byte 5001 next.

At the end of that exchange, both sides have exchanged and acknowledged each other's initial sequence numbers, the connection moves into an established state, and either side may now send application data. In fact, that third segment does not have to be empty, if the client already has data ready to send, it can attach it to that same ACK segment rather than sending it separately. It is also worth noticing that the two directions of the connection are entirely independent counters, the client's sequence numbers and the server's sequence numbers have nothing to do with each other, each side simply tracks, in its own acknowledgment field, what it next expects from the other.

This handshake is the foundation everything downstream relies on. Once both initial sequence numbers are agreed upon here, every acknowledgment, every retransmission, and every window calculation covered in the chapters ahead can be expressed simply as an offset from the starting points fixed during these three segments.
